guides.description: The ERGOEXP opt-in gate — what it means, how to opt in, and why it exists.
guides.body:
Some APIs ship before their shape has settled. Rather than hold a release for them or let
them quietly become de-facto stable, Ergosfare marks them `[Experimental]` with a diagnostic
ID prefixed `ERGOEXP`.

Consuming one is a **compile-time error** until you opt in explicitly.

## What the marking means

An `[Experimental]` API is **outside the compatibility promise**
([COMPATIBILITY.md §4](https://github.com/stellayazilim/ergosfare/blob/main/COMPATIBILITY.md)).
It may change signature, change behaviour, or disappear in any release — including a patch
release. Nothing about the normal deprecation cycle applies.

## Opting in

Per call site, which is the form to prefer because it documents itself:

```csharp
#pragma warning disable ERGOEXP001 // opting into an experimental API
var thing = new SomeExperimentalType();
#pragma warning restore ERGOEXP001
```

Or per project, when you have decided to accept the API across the board:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);ERGOEXP001</NoWarn>
</PropertyGroup>
```

Each experimental API gets its own ID, so opting into one never opts you into another.

## Current experimental surface

**`ERGOEXP001` — the declarative result-adapter surface.** `[ResultAdapter]`,
`[IgnoreResultAdapter]`, and `IModuleRegistry.UseDefaultResultAdapter(...)` with its
`DefaultResultAdapter` carrier.

The value channel's *semantics* are settled — a handler returning a value-carried failure has
that failure surfaced out of the pipeline without throwing. What is young is the **binding**
surface: how a message declares which adapter serves it, and how an application configures a
fallback. Those shapes may still shift in a minor release, so the gate stays on until they
have been used enough to settle.

The generator validates the binding at compile time regardless — `ERGOSG011` through
`ERGOSG014` catch an adapter that can never bind, conflicting annotations, and a result type
the configured default cannot serve. See
[Configuring](/ergosfare.docs/getting-started/configuring#result-adapters).

## Why a gate rather than a preview branch

The v2 line uses **rolling graduation**: features mature on `preview` and graduate to stable
individually, with no big-bang release-candidate freeze. That works only if a genuinely
unstable API can ship without blocking everything around it.

The `[Experimental]` gate is what makes that safe. An unfinished API can go out and be used
by people who want it, while the opt-in makes the risk explicit at every call site — so it
never accumulates silent dependents that a later change would break.

## Experimental is not preview

Two different things, easy to conflate:

| | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **The preview line** | A whole release train that has not settled yet. APIs may change between previews; that is what "preview" means. |
| **`[Experimental]`** | A specific API that is unstable *even relative to the line it ships on*. v2 being stable does not make its experimental APIs stable — they stay behind the gate until they graduate. |

An API can be experimental on a stable release. That is the point of the gate.

See [Versioning and release model](https://github.com/stellayazilim/ergosfare#versioning--release-model)
for the branch and tag rules.

guides.title: Performance
guides.description: Where the time and allocation savings come from, the measured per-dispatch numbers, and how to read them honestly.
guides.body:
The design premise is that all dispatch-shape work happens at compile time or once per
message type, never per dispatch. This page shows what that buys and what it does not.

## Where the work goes

**Compile time.** The source generator compiles the frozen composition table and emits
dispatch roots that close the runtime's generic executor and invoker types over each message.
Nothing has to be discovered or constructed at startup.

**Once per `(message type, group set)`.** The pipeline plan is built and cached process-wide:
six fixed stages, each a pre-ordered array, with covariant matching resolved and generic
handler types already closed. Group filters and `[ExcludeFromPipeline]` are applied here,
once.

**Every dispatch.** Rent a pooled context, look up the cached executor for the message's
runtime type, walk the plan, resolve handler *instances* from the calling scope, return the
context. No reflection, no `MakeGenericType`, no assembly scan, no `AsyncLocal`.

The executor holds its own resolved plan. Because the composition table is frozen, there is no
version to re-validate and no invalidation path — a selection made before the container was
built cannot change afterwards. Group-less dispatch, which is nearly all of it, is keyed by
message type alone, so no group set is materialized and no composite key is hashed.

## Pooled contexts

Execution contexts are rented from a `[ThreadStatic]`-first pool — a plain load and store on
the common same-thread cycle — and returned on completion. A synchronous fast path skips the
async state machine entirely when the whole pipeline completes synchronously.

This is the single largest contributor to the allocation numbers below, and it is the source
of the one rule the API imposes: a pooled context is valid only for the duration of its
dispatch. See
[Execution context](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/execution-context#pooling-and-the-lifetime-rule).

## Typed all the way down

Executors and invokers are closed over each message's concrete runtime type, so handlers are
invoked through their typed members with no object-typed bridge anywhere. `MakeGenericType`
survives only as a fallback for message types without a generated root, chiefly open generics.

## Generated plans

Single-handler command and query pipelines receive **generated plans**: straight-line typed
calls with no strategy object and no interceptor-count checks. Eligible transient handlers can
go further and receive direct-construction factories — including provider-based factories for
constructor dependencies — while runtime gates preserve the configured DI lifetime and any
`ForceMemoizedHandlers()` override.

Interceptor-bearing pipelines receive generated **staged** plans covering the pre, handler,
post, exception and final stages. When a composition does not match what a plan assumes, only
the optimization is given up: dispatch falls back to the general executor and the result is
unchanged.

## Mediator lifetime

The mediator facades — `ICommandMediator`, `IQueryMediator`, `IEventMediator`,
`IMessageMediator` — are registered **transient**. They are stateless; the only thing they
capture is the provider that resolved them, and a transient service receives the resolving
scope's provider exactly as a scoped one does. Handlers still resolve from the calling scope.

The difference is what registration costs. Resolving a scoped service takes the scope's lock
and writes the instance into the scope's resolved-services dictionary — a cost that amortizes
across a long-lived scope, and never amortizes at all when every dispatch gets its own scope.
That is the request-shaped case, and it is why these facades are transient.

## Measured shapes

Per-dispatch, with `[MemoryDiagnoser]`, on the v2.7.0-preview benchmark tree
(.NET 9.0.11, AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D):

| Shape | Mean | Allocated |
|---|---:|---:|
| Generated no-result command | 19.9 ns | 24 B |
| Generated result query | 24.0 ns | 24 B |
| Five-participant query pipeline | 120.2 ns | 96 B |
| Two-subscriber event | 50.5 ns | 48 B |

Request-shaped rows — the ones that create a DI scope per dispatch and resolve a mediator
inside it — stayed ahead of the equivalent MediatR rows.

Reproduce with:

```bash
dotnet run -c Release -f net9.0 --project test/Stella.Ergosfare.Benchmarking
```

{% aside type="note" %}
**The cross-library comparison table is being re-measured.** The benchmark project was
restructured for per-dispatch shapes during the v2 preview cycle, and the published
side-by-side table predates that. Rather than carry numbers whose benchmark methods no longer
exist, this page states only what was measured on the current shape. The comparison returns
when it has been re-run against the v2.3.0 tree.
{% /aside %}

## Reading these honestly

**They are a floor, not a forecast.** A no-op handler in a tight loop measures the dispatch
machinery and nothing else. Your handler does work; that work will dominate, and a 20 ns
dispatch is noise beside a database round trip. What the numbers tell you is that the mediator
is not where your latency goes.

**Allocation is the durable margin.** Pooled contexts, a `ValueTask`-first surface and
generated plans keep per-dispatch allocation in the tens of bytes. Time margins move with the
machine, the JIT and the DI shape; the allocation shape moves far less.

**Transient handlers allocate on purpose.** One instance per dispatch is what a transient
registration declares. Dispatch-heavy single-scope loops that want instance reuse should
register handlers as singletons or call `ForceMemoizedHandlers()` — which drops scoped and
transient dependency semantics in exchange, so read
[Modules and extensions](/ergosfare.docs/core-components/modules-extensions#extension-points)
before reaching for it.

**Event publishing and streaming queries are their own shapes.** `PublishAsync` broadcasts to
every matching handler by design, and `StreamAsync` returns an enumerable the caller drains
after the call returns. Neither is described by the command and query rows above.

## Getting the most out of it

- Use [`RegisterGenerated()`](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/compile-time-discovery) — it is
  also the only registration path that produces generated plans and dispatch roots.
- Return `ValueTask` without `async` when the handler completes synchronously.
- Give handlers a single public constructor, so generated plans can construct them directly
  rather than falling back to the container (`ERGOSG003` tells you when they cannot).
- Register stateless handlers as singletons.
- Keep interceptors off high-volume messages with
  [`[ExcludeFromPipeline]`](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/groups-and-weights).
- Measure your own workload. These numbers are a no-op handler in a tight loop; yours is not.

Next: [Native AOT and trimming](/ergosfare.docs/advanced/aot-and-trimming).

guides.title: Defining a command
guides.description: ICommand and ICommand<TResult> — when a command returns something, and when it should not.
guides.body:
A command is a message that asks the system to *do* something. Declaring one means
implementing a marker interface — there is no base class and nothing to override.

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Commands.Abstractions;

public sealed record CreateProduct(string Name, decimal Price) : ICommand<Guid>;
```

That is the entire definition. The source generator finds it at compile time and includes it
in `RegisterGenerated()`.

## Two shapes

| Interface | Handler contract | Mediator returns |
|---|---|---|
| `ICommand` | `ICommandHandler<TCommand>` | `ValueTask` |
| `ICommand<TResult>` | `ICommandHandler<TCommand, TResult>` | `ValueTask<TResult>` |

```csharp
public sealed record DeleteProduct(Guid Id) : ICommand;              // no result
public sealed record CreateProduct(string Name) : ICommand<Guid>;    // returns the new id
```

Prefer `ICommand` when there is genuinely nothing to return. Returning `bool` for "it worked"
is noise — a failed command should throw, and the exception stage decides what the caller
sees.

## Records, not classes

Commands are data. `record` gives you value equality, a readable constructor, and `with`
expressions — which matter because
[pre-interceptors can rewrite a message](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/pre-interceptors#rewriting-the-message):

```csharp
public ValueTask<CreateProduct> HandleAsync(CreateProduct command, ErgosfareContext context)
    => ValueTask.FromResult(command with { Name = command.Name.Trim() });
```

`sealed` is worth the keystrokes too. An unsealed command participates in covariant matching
as a base type, which is occasionally what you want and usually a surprise.

`record struct` works and is fully supported, including under Native AOT — the generator
emits a dispatch root for it, which is what shared generic code cannot provide.

## Marker interfaces for cross-cutting behaviour

Because interceptors [match covariantly](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/polymorphism), an
interface on a group of commands is how you attach behaviour to all of them at once:

```csharp
public interface IAuditedCommand : ICommand;

public sealed record CreateProduct(string Name) : IAuditedCommand;
public sealed record DeleteProduct(Guid Id)     : IAuditedCommand;
```

One `ICommandPreInterceptor<IAuditedCommand>` now covers both, and every audited command
added later.

## Where commands live

A command usually belongs next to the code that handles it, but it does not have to. A
library can declare commands and handlers with no registration code at all — the consuming
application's generated registration picks them up across the assembly boundary. Such a
library needs only:

```bash
dotnet add package Stella.Ergosfare.Commands.Abstractions
```

See [Compile-time discovery](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/compile-time-discovery#cross-assembly-discovery).

## Controlling registration

- `[DiscoveryKey("…")]` gates the command out of default discovery until a registration call
  selects its key — see [Discovery keys](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/discovery-keys).
- `[ExcludeFromDiscovery]` removes it from automatic registration entirely.
- `[ExcludeFromPipeline]` keeps it out of covariantly matched interceptors — see
  [Groups and weights](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/groups-and-weights).

## Sending one

```csharp
var id = await _commands.SendAsync(new CreateProduct("Laptop", 999m));
await _commands.SendAsync(new DeleteProduct(id));
```

Both overloads accept an optional `CommandMediationSettings` and a `CancellationToken`, or an
`ErgosfareContext` when you are
[dispatching from inside a handler](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/nested-dispatch).

Next: [Defining a command handler](/ergosfare.docs/core-components/command/command-handler).

guides.title: Defining a command handler
guides.description: ICommandHandler, ValueTask returns, dependency injection, and the one handler per command rule.
guides.body:
A command handler implements `ICommandHandler<TCommand, TResult>` — or
`ICommandHandler<TCommand>` when the command produces nothing.

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Commands.Abstractions;
using Stella.Ergosfare.Core.Abstractions;

public sealed class CreateProductHandler : ICommandHandler<CreateProduct, Guid>
{
    private readonly IProductStore _store;

    public CreateProductHandler(IProductStore store) => _store = store;

    public ValueTask<Guid> HandleAsync(CreateProduct command, ErgosfareContext context)
        => _store.AddAsync(command.Name, command.Price, context.CancellationToken);
}
```

No attribute, no registration call. The source generator finds it.

## `ValueTask`, not `Task`

The whole surface is `ValueTask`-first. A handler that completes synchronously allocates
nothing — no `Task` object, no async state machine:

```csharp
public ValueTask<Guid> HandleAsync(CreateProduct command, ErgosfareContext context)
    => ValueTask.FromResult(Guid.NewGuid());          // zero allocations
```

Mark the method `async` only when you actually await:

```csharp
public async ValueTask<Guid> HandleAsync(CreateProduct command, ErgosfareContext context)
{
    var id = await _store.AddAsync(command.Name, command.Price, context.CancellationToken);
    await _outbox.QueueAsync(id, context.CancellationToken);
    return id;
}
```

{% aside type="caution" %}
Never await a `ValueTask` twice, and never store one. That is a `ValueTask` rule, not an
Ergosfare rule, but it bites more often here because the whole surface returns them.
{% /aside %}

## The context parameter

There is no `CancellationToken` parameter. It arrives on the context:

```csharp
context.CancellationToken
```

The context also carries the per-dispatch item bag, `Abort()`, and `CreateScope()` for
[nested dispatch](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/nested-dispatch). It deliberately exposes no
service provider — dependencies belong in the constructor.

See [Execution context](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/execution-context), including the rule
that a pooled context must not outlive its dispatch.

## Dependency injection and lifetimes

Handlers are resolved from the **calling DI scope** on every dispatch, so constructor
injection works exactly as it does anywhere else. The lifetime is whatever you registered:

| Registration | Per dispatch |
|---|---|
| Singleton | Container-cached; one instance for the process |
| Scoped | One instance per DI scope |
| Transient | A new instance every dispatch |

A transient handler allocating once per dispatch is not a leak — it is what a transient
registration declares. For dispatch-heavy loops inside one scope, register the handler as a
singleton or call `ForceMemoizedHandlers()` — see
[Configuring Ergosfare](/ergosfare.docs/getting-started/configuring#handler-lifetimes).

## One handler per command

A command has exactly one main handler. Registering two for the same command type is a
configuration error, and the runtime raises `MultipleHandlerFoundException` at dispatch.

If you want several things to happen, that is what
[events](/ergosfare.docs/core-components/event/event-definition) are for: publish one after
the command succeeds, and let any number of handlers react.

## Commands without a result

```csharp
public sealed record DeleteProduct(Guid Id) : ICommand;

public sealed class DeleteProductHandler : ICommandHandler<DeleteProduct>
{
    private readonly IProductStore _store;

    public DeleteProductHandler(IProductStore store) => _store = store;

    public ValueTask HandleAsync(DeleteProduct command, ErgosfareContext context)
        => _store.RemoveAsync(command.Id, context.CancellationToken);
}
```

## Handling a base type

Because the message type parameter is contravariant (`in TCommand`), a handler can be
declared against a base type or interface. For *commands* this is rarely what you want —
one handler per command is the rule, and a base-type handler competes with the specific
one. Covariant matching earns its keep for
[interceptors](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/interceptors) and for
[event handlers](/ergosfare.docs/core-components/event/event-handler).

## Failure

Throw. There is no result code to return and no need for one:

- [Exception interceptors](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/exception-interceptors)
  can translate the exception or supply a fallback result.
- [Final interceptors](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/final-interceptors) run either
  way, so cleanup is safe.

To refuse the work outright, call `context.Abort(reason)`. It cuts the pipeline where it
stands — no further stage runs, including the final one — and the caller receives
`ExecutionAbortedException`. It supplies no result, whatever the command declares; see
[Aborting](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/execution-context#aborting).

Next: [Defining a query](/ergosfare.docs/core-components/query/query-definition).

guides.title: Defining an event
guides.description: IEvent — broadcast to any number of handlers, including handlers registered against a base type.
guides.body:
An event states that something happened. Unlike a command, it is **broadcast**: any number of
handlers may react, including none.

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Events.Abstractions;

public sealed record ProductCreated(Guid Id, string Name) : IEvent;
```

There is one shape only — `IEvent`. An event has no result, because there is no single
handler whose answer would count.

## Commands versus events

| | Command | Event |
|---|---|---|
| Intent | do this | this happened |
| Handlers | exactly one | zero or more |
| Result | optional (`ICommand<TResult>`) | none |
| Naming | imperative — `CreateProduct` | past tense — `ProductCreated` |
| Adding a handler | a configuration error | the normal way to extend |

The past-tense naming is not decoration. If you find yourself wanting a result back from an
event, or wanting exactly one handler to own it, what you have is a command.

## Covariant broadcast

Event handlers match [covariantly](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/polymorphism). A handler
registered against a base type or interface receives every assignable event:

```csharp
public interface IDomainEvent : IEvent;

public sealed record ProductCreated(Guid Id, string Name) : IDomainEvent;
public sealed record ProductDeleted(Guid Id)              : IDomainEvent;

public sealed class AppendToOutbox : IEventHandler<IDomainEvent>
{
    public ValueTask HandleAsync(IDomainEvent @event, ErgosfareContext context)
        => _outbox.AppendAsync(@event, context.CancellationToken);
}
```

One registration, and every domain event added later is covered. Handlers registered for the
event's own type run **before** covariantly matched ones.

{% aside type="note" %}
Covariant delivery to event *handlers* is new in v2. On the v1 line only interceptors matched
covariantly — event handlers had to name the exact event type. See
[Migrating from v1](/ergosfare.docs/migration/v1-to-v2).
{% /aside %}

## Events carry data, not references

An event is often consumed after the fact — by an outbox, an audit log, a projection. Put the
values in it rather than an entity the handler has to reload against a `DbContext` that may
already be gone:

```csharp
public sealed record ProductCreated(Guid Id, string Name, decimal Price) : IEvent;   // good
public sealed record ProductCreated(Product Entity) : IEvent;                        // fragile
```

## Publishing

```csharp
await _events.PublishAsync(new ProductCreated(id, name));
```

The call completes when every matching handler has completed. `PublishAsync` takes an optional
`EventMediationSettings` and a `CancellationToken`, and has an `ErgosfareContext` overload
for [nested dispatch](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/nested-dispatch) — which is how you
publish from inside a command handler:

```csharp
public async ValueTask HandleAsync(PlaceOrder msg, ErgosfareContext ctx)
{
    using var scope = ctx.CreateScope();
    await _events.PublishAsync(new OrderPlaced(msg.OrderId), scope.Context);
}
```

## Controlling registration

`[DiscoveryKey]`, `[ExcludeFromDiscovery]` and `[ExcludeFromPipeline]` apply to events as to
any other message. `[ExcludeFromPipeline]` is particularly useful on high-frequency events
that should not go through the blanket interceptors — it affects covariantly matched
*interceptors*, never handlers.

Next: [Defining an event handler](/ergosfare.docs/core-components/event/event-handler).

guides.title: Defining an event handler
guides.description: IEventHandler — many handlers per event, what happens when one throws, and why handlers must not depend on each other.

guides.title: Modules and extensions
guides.description: The three shipped modules, the packages each one spans, and how the core, abstractions and DI layers divide the work.
guides.body:
Ergosfare ships three modules — Commands, Queries and Events — over a shared core. Each is
independent: you register the ones you use and pay for nothing else.

| Module | Message | Handler | Mediator | Dispatch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Commands | `ICommand`, `ICommand<TResult>` | `ICommandHandler<…>` | `ICommandMediator` | `SendAsync` |
| Queries | `IQuery<TResult>`, `IStreamQuery<TResult>` | `IQueryHandler<…>`, `IStreamQueryHandler<…>` | `IQueryMediator` | `QueryAsync`, `StreamAsync` |
| Events | `IEvent`, and any `notnull` type | `IEventHandler<TEvent>` | `IEventMediator` | `PublishAsync` |

They differ only in cardinality and result shape. All three run through the same frozen
composition table, the same pipeline plan and the same four
[interceptor stages](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/interceptors).

The event module is also the open lane for plain messages: `IEventHandler<TEvent>` constrains
`TEvent` to `notnull` and nothing else, so a POCO publishes without implementing `IEvent`.

## The three layers

Every module spans the same three packages, and the split is worth understanding because it
decides what a given project has to reference.

**`*.Abstractions`** — the contracts. `ICommand`, `ICommandHandler<…>`, the interceptor
interfaces, the mediation settings. No runtime, no DI container. This is all a library needs
to declare messages and handlers.

**`Stella.Ergosfare.*`** — the runtime for that module: the mediator implementation and the
invoker caches that close generics over each message's runtime type.

**`*.Extensions.MicrosoftDependencyInjection`** — the registration surface: the module
builder, `AddCommandModule` and friends. This is the only layer that knows about
`IServiceCollection`, which is what keeps the rest container-agnostic.

`Stella.Ergosfare.Core.Abstractions` sits under all of them and holds what is not
module-specific: `ErgosfareContext`, the `[DiscoveryKey]`/`[Group]`/`[Weight]` attributes,
the handler and interceptor base contracts, and the frozen composition table with its
dispatch roots.

The umbrella package `Stella.Ergosfare` is a convenience bundle over all three modules. See
[Installation](/ergosfare.docs/getting-started/installation) for choosing deliberately.

## Registering modules

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(o => o
    .AddCommandModule(c => c.RegisterGenerated())
    .AddQueryModule(q => q.RegisterGenerated())
    .AddEventModule(e => e.RegisterGenerated()));
```

Each `AddXModule` constructs a module, hands it your registration lambda, and registers the
module's mediator with `TryAddTransient` — so calling it twice is harmless. The facades are
transient because they are stateless and a transient still resolves against the calling
scope; see [Performance](/ergosfare.docs/advanced/performance#mediator-lifetime).

Only add what you use. An application that never publishes events should not register the
event module; `IEventMediator` then simply is not resolvable, which is a better failure than
a silent no-op.

## Extension points

**`ForceMemoizedHandlers()`** on the registry resolves every handler graph once and memoizes
it process-wide, for dispatch-heavy loops with transient handlers. It is the fastest dispatch
mode and it does **not** honour scoped or transient handler dependencies — the first resolved
instance serves every later dispatch:

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(o => o
    .ForceMemoizedHandlers()
    .AddCommandModule(c => c.RegisterGenerated()));
```

Without the switch, registered lifetimes are honoured, and messages whose participants are
all singletons take the memoized path automatically.

**`UseDefaultResultAdapter(...)`** sets the fallback `IResultAdapter` for result slots that
bind nothing more specific:

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(o => o
    .UseDefaultResultAdapter(typeof(MyResultAdapter<>))
    .AddQueryModule(q => q.RegisterGenerated()));
```

This surface is `[Experimental]` under `ERGOEXP001`; see
[Configuring](/ergosfare.docs/getting-started/configuring#result-adapters).

**Your own `IModule`** — the modules above are not privileged. Implementing `IModule` gives
you a new message shape on the same machinery, selected from the same compiled table; see
[Modules and plugins](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/plugins).

## Mediators are per-module on purpose

There is no single `IMediator`. A component takes the narrow interface it needs, and the
type system does the rest: something holding only `IQueryMediator` cannot send a command or
publish an event. That is the cheapest CQRS boundary available, and it costs one extra
constructor parameter when a class genuinely needs two.

Next: [Defining a command](/ergosfare.docs/core-components/command/command-definition).

guides.title: Defining a query
guides.description: IQuery<TResult> for a single result, IStreamQuery<TResult> for a stream — and why queries always return something.
guides.body:
A query asks the system for data. Unlike a command, it **always** produces a result — there
is no result-less query interface, because a query that returns nothing has nothing to say.

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Queries.Abstractions;

public sealed record GetProduct(Guid Id) : IQuery<Product?>;
```

## Two shapes

| Interface | Handler contract | Mediator call | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `IQuery<TResult>` | `IQueryHandler<TQuery, TResult>` | `QueryAsync` | `ValueTask<TResult>` |
| `IStreamQuery<TResult>` | `IStreamQueryHandler<TQuery, TResult>` | `StreamAsync` | `IAsyncEnumerable<TResult>` |

```csharp
public sealed record GetProduct(Guid Id) : IQuery<Product?>;
public sealed record StreamProducts(int PageSize) : IStreamQuery<Product>;
```

Use `IStreamQuery<TResult>` when the result set is large enough that materialising it costs
more than you want to pay, or when the consumer can start work before the last row arrives.

## Nullability is part of the contract

`IQuery<Product?>` and `IQuery<Product>` say different things. The first admits "not found"
as a normal outcome; the second promises a result and should throw when it cannot deliver
one. Pick deliberately — the handler signature follows from it, and so does what callers have
to write.

## Records, sealed, and marker interfaces

The same guidance as for [commands](/ergosfare.docs/core-components/command/command-definition)
applies:

- `record` for value equality and `with` expressions, which
  [pre-interceptors](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/pre-interceptors) use to rewrite.
- `sealed` unless you intend the query to be a covariant base.
- A shared interface when you want one interceptor to cover a family:

```csharp
public interface ICacheableQuery : IQuery;

public sealed record GetProduct(Guid Id) : ICacheableQuery, IQuery<Product?>;
```

One `IQueryPreInterceptor<ICacheableQuery>` can then serve every cacheable query.

## Queries should not mutate

Nothing in the framework enforces this — the separation is yours to keep. What the framework
does give you is a mediator per module: a component that takes `IQueryMediator` and not
`ICommandMediator` *cannot* send commands. Injecting the narrow interface is the enforcement
mechanism.

## Controlling registration

`[DiscoveryKey]`, `[ExcludeFromDiscovery]` and `[ExcludeFromPipeline]` work on queries
exactly as on commands. See [Discovery keys](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/discovery-keys)
and [Groups and weights](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/groups-and-weights).

## Dispatching one

```csharp
var product  = await _queries.QueryAsync(new GetProduct(id));

await foreach (var p in _queries.StreamAsync(new StreamProducts(100)))
    Console.WriteLine(p.Name);
```

Both take an optional `QueryMediationSettings` and a `CancellationToken`, and `QueryAsync`
has an `ErgosfareContext` overload for
[nested dispatch](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/nested-dispatch).

Next: [Defining a query handler](/ergosfare.docs/core-components/query/query-handler).

guides.title: Compile-time discovery
guides.description: How the Ergosfare source generator finds handlers, what it emits, and how to control it.
guides.body:
Most mediators discover handlers by reflecting over assemblies at startup. Ergosfare does it
at compile time: a Roslyn source generator walks your compilation, finds everything
registrable, compiles the relationships into a **frozen composition table**, and writes a
registration method into your project.

The result is a startup path with **no reflection over handler types at all**, and a build
where the compiler — not the runtime — tells you if something cannot be registered. This is
the only discovery path: since v2.3 there is no runtime scanning to fall back to.

## What the generator emits

After a build, look in:

```
obj/gen/Stella.Ergosfare.SourceGenerator/…/ErgosfareRegistrations.g.cs
```

You will find an `internal static class ErgosfareGeneratedRegistrations` in namespace
`Stella.Ergosfare.Generated`, carrying extension methods on each module builder:

```csharp
namespace Stella.Ergosfare.Generated
{
    internal static class ErgosfareGeneratedRegistrations
    {
        public static CommandModuleBuilder RegisterGenerated(this CommandModuleBuilder builder);
        public static CommandModuleBuilder RegisterGenerated(this CommandModuleBuilder builder, string discoveryKeyPattern);
        // …the same pair for QueryModuleBuilder and EventModuleBuilder
    }
}
```

This is why `RegisterGenerated()` appears in no NuGet package and in no API reference: it
does not exist until your project compiles. It is generated *per compilation*, already
containing your handlers.

{% aside type="tip" %}
The class is `internal`, so `RegisterGenerated()` is only callable from the project that
generated it. Each application generates its own.
{% /aside %}

## Using it

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Generated;

builder.Services.AddErgosfare(o => o
    .AddCommandModule(c => c.RegisterGenerated())
    .AddQueryModule(q => q.RegisterGenerated())
    .AddEventModule(e => e.RegisterGenerated()));
```

A missing `using Stella.Ergosfare.Generated;` is the single most common reason
`RegisterGenerated()` fails to resolve.

## What counts as registrable

The generator looks for concrete, non-abstract types implementing any of:

- a handler contract — `ICommandHandler<…>`, `IQueryHandler<…>`, `IStreamQueryHandler<…>`, `IEventHandler<…>`
- an interceptor contract — pre, post, exception or final, in any of their arities
- a message contract — `ICommand`, `ICommand<TResult>`, `IQuery<TResult>`, `IStreamQuery<TResult>`, `IEvent`

Messages matter as much as handlers: the generator uses them to emit **dispatch roots**.

## Dispatch roots

For every dispatchable message the generator emits a static reference that closes the
runtime's generic executor and invoker types over that message:

```csharp
GeneratedDispatchRoots.AddMessage<CreateProduct>();
GeneratedDispatchRoots.AddResult<CreateProduct, Guid>();
```

Two things fall out of this:

- The runtime constructs executors without `MakeGenericType`. That call survives only as a
  fallback for message types without a generated root, chiefly open generics.
- Native AOT gets a **static anchor for every generic instantiation** — including
  `record struct` messages, which shared generic code cannot cover and which would otherwise
  fail at runtime in a trimmed build.

Dispatch-root additions are idempotent, so every registration surface calls them
unconditionally.

## Cross-assembly discovery

The generator also walks **referenced assemblies**. A library that ships handlers needs no
registration code of its own — its handlers register through the consuming application's
generated code:

```csharp
// In a class library. No AddErgosfare, no registration code, nothing.
public sealed record LibGreet(string Name) : ICommand<string>;

public sealed class LibGreetHandler : ICommandHandler<LibGreet, string>
{
    public ValueTask<string> HandleAsync(LibGreet message, ErgosfareContext context)
        => new($"lib says hi, {message.Name}");
}
```

The application's `RegisterGenerated()` picks it up.

Internal types in a referenced assembly participate when that assembly grants
`InternalsVisibleTo` to the consuming project.

To turn reference scanning off for a project:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <ErgosfareSourceGeneratorScanReferences>false</ErgosfareSourceGeneratorScanReferences>
</PropertyGroup>
```

### Assemblies under the `Stella.Ergosfare.*` prefix

Reference scanning skips assemblies whose name begins with `Stella.Ergosfare` — that prefix
is the library's own, and its contract interfaces (`ICommandHandler<T>` and friends) inherit
the module markers, so scanning them would register the framework's own types. If you
deliberately name an application assembly under that prefix, opt it back in:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <ErgosfareSourceGeneratorForceScanReferences>true</ErgosfareSourceGeneratorForceScanReferences>
</PropertyGroup>
```

The property is baked into the assembly as
`[assembly: AssemblyMetadata("ErgosfareSourceGeneratorForceScanReferences", "true")]`, which
the generator reads per referenced assembly. Only assemblies that set it are force-included,
so the library's own contracts are never scanned — even though they share the prefix.

## Diagnostics

Because discovery happens at compile time, the generator can see problems a runtime scanner
could only fail on. It reports them rather than registering something surprising.

**Visibility — the type cannot be named**

| ID | Severity | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ERGOSG001` | Warning | A registrable type in this compilation is private, protected or file-local, so generated registration cannot name it. |
| `ERGOSG002` | Warning | A registrable type in a referenced assembly is not visible — usually internal without `InternalsVisibleTo`. |

**Reachability — the dispatch and the handler do not meet**

| ID | Severity | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ERGOSG005` | Error | This dispatch can never reach a handler: nothing in the closure handles the message or any of its subtypes. It would throw `NoHandlerFoundException`. |
| `ERGOSG006` | Warning | The dispatched static type has no covering handler; only subtypes are handled. |
| `ERGOSG007` | Warning | A handler exists that no dispatch site in the closure can deliver to. |
| `ERGOSG008` | Info | An unreachable handler was trimmed out of generated registration. |
| `ERGOSG009` | Info | The dispatch site's static message type is opaque, so nothing can be proved about it. |
| `ERGOSG010` | Error | Several main handlers claim the same message at the same priority level — see [Polymorphism](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/polymorphism). |

**Construction — the plan falls back to the container**

| ID | Severity | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ERGOSG003` | Info | The handler has more than one public constructor, so generated plans cannot prove which to call and keep it on the container path. |
| `ERGOSG004` | Info | `[FromServices]` on a constructor parameter has no effect — constructor injection already resolves from the container. |

**Result adapters** (the `ERGOEXP001` surface)

| ID | Severity | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ERGOSG011` | Error | The `[ResultAdapter]` declared on a message can never bind to its declared result type. |
| `ERGOSG012` | Error | A message carries both `[ResultAdapter]` and `[IgnoreResultAdapter]`. |
| `ERGOSG013` | Error | The message's result type is not served by the configured default adapter. |
| `ERGOSG014` | Warning | An opted-out message keeps a throwing pipeline while the default adapter cannot serve its result. |

Take the warnings seriously — a handler that silently never runs is worse than a build break.

## The composition root

The reachability diagnostics (`ERGOSG005`–`ERGOSG008`) only mean anything where the closure is
complete: a library compiled on its own cannot know which of its handlers the application will
dispatch to. So the generator judges reachability in the **composition root** — by default, any
project whose output is an executable. Libraries are not judged.

Override it when the default guesses wrong:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <!-- a library that composes the final pipeline: judge it -->
  <ErgosfareCompositionRoot>true</ErgosfareCompositionRoot>

  <!-- an executable that is not the real root (a test host, a tool): stay quiet -->
  <ErgosfareCompositionRoot>false</ErgosfareCompositionRoot>
</PropertyGroup>
```

## Trimming unreachable handlers

In a composition root, a handler no dispatch site can reach is dead weight the linker cannot
prove is dead — it is named by generated registration, so it stays. Opt in and the generator
stops naming it:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <ErgosfareTrimUnusedHandlers>true</ErgosfareTrimUnusedHandlers>
</PropertyGroup>
```

Each trimmed handler is reported as `ERGOSG008` (Info), so the build still says what it
dropped. This is opt-in for a reason: the judgment is only as complete as the dispatch
manifests, and a handler reached through a path the generator cannot see would be trimmed out
of a build that needs it. Leave it off unless you are chasing size in a
[trimmed or AOT publish](/ergosfare.docs/advanced/aot-and-trimming), where `ERGOSG007` is
already telling you the handler is unreachable.

## There is no runtime scanning

`RegisterFromAssembly(assembly)` was removed in v2.3. An assembly loaded with
`Assembly.LoadFrom` after compilation cannot append a message shape to the frozen composition
table, and `Register<T>()` selects only types the table already holds.

A genuine plugin host has one supported shape: compile the plugin contracts into the closure
the generator sees, and let the host choose at registration time which of them to select —
with `RegisterGenerated(pattern)` over [discovery keys](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/discovery-keys),
or explicit `Register<T>()` calls behind your own feature flag.

Next: [Discovery keys](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/discovery-keys) — registering only part
of what was discovered.

guides.title: Discovery keys
guides.description: Gate handlers behind named keys so registration can cherry-pick which discovered types actually register.
guides.body:
Compile-time discovery finds everything. Discovery keys decide what actually **registers**.

A type tagged with `[DiscoveryKey]` is *excluded from default discovery* and registers only
when a registration call names one of its keys. That turns "which handlers exist" (a compile
time question) and "which handlers are active" (a deployment question) into two separate
decisions, without reflection and without conditional compilation.

## The default key

Every untagged type carries the implicit **default key**, the empty string. That is exactly
what a pattern-less registration call selects:

```csharp
.AddCommandModule(c => c.RegisterGenerated())      // selects the default key only
```

So adding `[DiscoveryKey("reporting.daily")]` to a handler removes it from that call.

## Gating a handler

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Core.Abstractions.Attributes;

[DiscoveryKey("reporting.daily")]
public sealed class DailyReportHandler : ICommandHandler<BuildDailyReport>
{
    public ValueTask HandleAsync(BuildDailyReport command, ErgosfareContext context)
        => _reports.BuildAsync(context.CancellationToken);
}
```

```csharp
builder.Services.AddErgosfare(o => o
    .AddCommandModule(c => c
        .RegisterGenerated()                    // default discovery: untagged types
        .RegisterGenerated("reporting.*")));    // plus everything keyed under reporting
```

Calls compose. Overlapping patterns are safe — registration is idempotent.

## Patterns

A registration call accepts either an exact key or a trailing-`*` prefix glob:

| Pattern | Selects |
|---|---|
| `""` (or no argument) | Untagged types only |
| `"reporting.daily"` | Exactly that key |
| `"reporting.*"` | `reporting.daily`, `reporting.monthly`, `reporting.anything` |
| `"*"` | Every keyed type |

## Staying in default discovery *and* being selectable

List the empty string alongside your keys:

```csharp
[DiscoveryKey("", "debug")]
public sealed class VerboseLoggingInterceptor : ICommandPreInterceptor { … }
```

This registers under a plain `RegisterGenerated()` **and** under `RegisterGenerated("debug")`.

## Tagging a whole assembly

Applied at assembly level, the attribute sets the default keys for every registrable type in
that assembly that does not declare its own:

```csharp
[assembly: DiscoveryKey("payments")]
```

This is the modular-monolith case: a slice tags its entire surface in one place, and the host
opts the slice in with a single `RegisterGenerated("payments")`.

A type that declares its own `[DiscoveryKey]` overrides the assembly-level one — it does not
merge with it.

## Removing a type entirely

`[ExcludeFromDiscovery]` takes a type (or an assembly) out of discovery altogether. No key
pattern will select it:

```csharp
[ExcludeFromDiscovery]
public sealed class ExperimentalHandler : ICommandHandler<Probe> { … }
```

Explicit registration still works — `Register<ExperimentalHandler>()` selects it — which is
the intended escape hatch for something you want available but never automatic.

The reason it works is that `[ExcludeFromDiscovery]` shapes *discovery*, not the table. The
generator still emits the type's composition row; it is simply left out of every bulk
`RegisterGenerated()` call, so only a container that names the type runs it.

## Keys are the plugin story

Since v2.3 there is no runtime assembly scan, so discovery keys carry the whole "compile
everything, run some of it" pattern. The keyed slice is compiled into the closure like any
other code, and the host decides at registration time — from configuration, a feature flag,
an environment name — which patterns to select.

## When to reach for this

- **Feature flags at deployment time** — key the handlers, select by key from configuration.
- **Environment-specific interceptors** — a `[DiscoveryKey("debug")]` interceptor that only
  a development host registers.
- **Modular monoliths** — one assembly-level key per slice, one registration call per slice
  the host wants to run.

What discovery keys are *not* for: filtering which handlers run for a particular dispatch.
That is a runtime concern and belongs to
[groups](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/groups-and-weights). Discovery keys are
decided once, at registration.

Next: [Polymorphism](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/polymorphism).

guides.title: Polymorphism
guides.description: Covariant handler and interceptor matching, direct-before-indirect ordering, and how event broadcast uses both.
guides.body:
A handler or interceptor registered against a base type or interface applies to **every
message assignable to it**. Ergosfare resolves this when it builds the pipeline plan — once
per message type — so covariant matching costs nothing per dispatch.

## Why it matters

Without covariance, a logging interceptor has to be registered once per command type, or take
`object` and lose all type information. With it, one registration covers a hierarchy:

```csharp
public interface IAuditedCommand : ICommand;

public sealed record CreateProduct(string Name) : IAuditedCommand;
public sealed record DeleteProduct(Guid Id)    : IAuditedCommand;
public sealed record Heartbeat()               : ICommand;      // not audited

public sealed class AuditTrail : ICommandPreInterceptor<IAuditedCommand>
{
    public ValueTask<IAuditedCommand> HandleAsync(IAuditedCommand command, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        _audit.Log(command);
        return ValueTask.FromResult(command);
    }
}
```

`CreateProduct` and `DeleteProduct` go through `AuditTrail`. `Heartbeat` does not.

## Direct before indirect

Within a pipeline stage, entries fall into two groups:

- **Direct** — registered against the message's own type.
- **Indirect (covariant)** — registered against a base type or interface of the message.

Direct entries always run first. Within each group, `[Weight]` orders descending. The
ordering is computed when the plan is built, so it is stable and identical for every dispatch
of that message type.

```
CreateProduct pre-interceptors, in order:
  1. ICommandPreInterceptor<CreateProduct>        [Weight(50)]   ← direct
  2. ICommandPreInterceptor<CreateProduct>        [Weight(10)]   ← direct
  3. ICommandPreInterceptor<IAuditedCommand>      [Weight(99)]   ← indirect
  4. ICommandPreInterceptor                       [Weight(0)]    ← indirect
```

Note that the high-weight indirect interceptor still runs after the low-weight direct one.
Weight orders *within* a group, it does not promote across groups.

## Main handlers use a ladder, not an order

Interceptors and event handlers all run, so "direct first, then indirect" is enough. A command
or a single-handler query has exactly one main handler, so the same two groups become a
**priority ladder**:

1. **A sole direct handler wins outright** — however many covariant candidates exist. A
   supertype handler is a fallback, not a competitor.
2. **With no direct handler, the covariant level serves** — a handler registered against a
   base type or interface handles the assignable message.
3. **More than one candidate at the same level is a contest.** The count is taken before
   anything resolves, so a contested message runs *neither* claimant and the caller gets
   `MultipleHandlerFoundException`.
4. **Neither level populated** raises `NoHandlerFoundException`, which derives from
   `InvalidOperationException` and carries the `MessageType`.

```csharp
public sealed class CreateProductHandler  : ICommandHandler<CreateProduct, Guid> { … }  // direct
public sealed class AuditedFallback       : ICommandHandler<IAuditedCommand, Guid> { … } // covariant

// CreateProduct → CreateProductHandler. No contest: different levels.
```

Two handlers for `CreateProduct` itself, or two covariant handlers with no direct one, is the
contest case. The generator sees this at compile time and reports `ERGOSG010` rather than
leaving it to the first dispatch.

## Contravariance in handler contracts

The message type parameter on handler and interceptor contracts is declared `in`:

```csharp
public interface ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> : …
public interface IAsyncPreInterceptor<in TMessage> : …
```

That is what makes a handler for a base type usable where a derived message is expected. The
generic variance is enforced by the compiler; Ergosfare's plan builder just walks the type's
assignability graph to find matches.

## Events broadcast covariantly too

Event publication delivers to every matching handler, not just the ones registered against
the exact event type:

```csharp
public interface IDomainEvent : IEvent;

public sealed record OrderPlaced(Guid Id) : IDomainEvent;

public sealed class SendConfirmation : IEventHandler<OrderPlaced>  { … }  // direct
public sealed class AppendToOutbox   : IEventHandler<IDomainEvent> { … }  // indirect
```

Publishing an `OrderPlaced` runs `SendConfirmation` first, then `AppendToOutbox` — the same
direct-before-indirect rule as interceptors.

{% aside type="note" %}
Covariant delivery to *handlers* is new in v2. On the v1 line, only interceptors matched
covariantly; event handlers had to be registered against the exact event type. See
[Migrating from v1](/ergosfare.docs/migration/v1-to-v2).
{% /aside %}

An outbox or an audit sink registered against `IDomainEvent` therefore sees every domain
event with one registration — which is usually what you want, and occasionally not.

## Opting out

When a message should skip covariantly matched interceptors, mark the message:

```csharp
[ExcludeFromPipeline]
public sealed record Heartbeat : ICommand;
```

`Heartbeat` no longer picks up the blanket `ICommandPreInterceptor`. Interceptors registered
against `Heartbeat` itself still run — those were written for it deliberately — and main
handlers are never affected.

Scoping the exclusion to particular groups is also possible:

```csharp
[ExcludeFromPipeline("logging", "metrics")]
public sealed record Tick : ICommand;
```

See [Groups and weights](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/groups-and-weights).

## Cost

None per dispatch. Assignability is walked once, when the plan for a `(message type, group
set)` pair is first built; every later dispatch of that shape reads a pre-ordered array. The
generic handler types involved are closed at that same moment, so invocation goes through
typed members with no object-typed bridge.

Next: [Plugins](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/plugins).

guides.title: Exception interceptors
guides.description: Turning failures into results, translating exceptions, and deciding what propagates to the caller.
guides.body:
An exception interceptor runs when the handler — or anything earlier in the pipeline — threw.
It receives the message, whatever result had been produced so far, and the exception, and it
decides what the caller sees.

```csharp
public sealed class TranslateNotFound : IQueryExceptionInterceptor<GetProduct, Product?>
{
    public ValueTask<Product?> HandleAsync(
        GetProduct query, Product? result, Exception exception, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        if (exception is KeyNotFoundException)
            return ValueTask.FromResult<Product?>(null);

        throw exception;      // not ours — let it propagate
    }
}
```

Two outcomes, and nothing in between:

- **Return a value** — the exception is considered handled, and the caller receives that value.
- **Throw** — the exception propagates. Rethrow the original when it is not yours to handle.

## Where it sits

```
pre*  →  main handler  →  post*        →  final*
                       ↘  exception*  ↗
```

Post-interceptors do not run when the pipeline threw; the exception stage takes their place.
Final interceptors run either way — but neither stage runs after an
[abort](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/execution-context#aborting).

## Declaring the exception type

There are two contract families, and they are alternatives — not a replacement and a legacy
form. The untyped contracts above receive **every** exception and decide for themselves; the
`...For<TException>` contracts declare one type up front and run only for it:

```csharp
public sealed class TranslateNotFound
    : IQueryExceptionInterceptorFor<GetProduct, Product?, KeyNotFoundException>
{
    public ValueTask<Product?> HandleAsync(
        GetProduct query, Product? result, KeyNotFoundException exception, ErgosfareContext context)
        => ValueTask.FromResult<Product?>(null);
}
```

The exception arrives already typed, so the `is` check and the rethrow-what-isn't-mine line
both disappear. Matching follows `catch` semantics: a `TException` of `HttpRequestException`
accepts its derived types too. Each module carries the same three arities as the untyped
family — `...For<TException>`, `...For<TMessage, TException>` and
`...For<TMessage, TResult, TException>`.

**Which to reach for:**

| | Use |
|---|---|
| One exception type per interceptor | `...For<TException>` — the filter is the contract, and nothing can forget to rethrow |
| Several exception types in **one** interceptor | the untyped contracts — switch on the exception yourself, and rethrow what you do not handle |
| Logging or enriching every failure | the untyped contracts — a blanket interceptor is exactly the point |

Ordering does not change between them: `[Weight]` decides who runs, the filter only decides
who is *eligible*.

{% aside type="tip" %}
The typed family sharpens what "handled" means. Previously, having any exception interceptor
registered meant the exception could be swallowed; now **an exception is swallowed only when
an interceptor that actually matched it returns a value.** A pipeline whose only exception
interceptor filters on a type that did not occur leaves the original exception, and its stack,
entirely untouched — the forgotten `throw` in an untyped interceptor cannot silently eat a
failure any more, because a typed one never sees it in the first place.
{% /aside %}

## Logging without swallowing

The common case is enriching the failure and letting it continue:

```csharp
public sealed class LogFailures : ICommandExceptionInterceptor
{
    private readonly ILogger<LogFailures> _logger;

    public LogFailures(ILogger<LogFailures> logger) => _logger = logger;

    public ValueTask<object?> HandleAsync(
        ICommand command, object? result, Exception exception, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        _logger.LogError(exception, "{Command} failed", command.GetType().Name);
        throw exception;
    }
}
```

{% aside type="caution" %}
Returning a value from an exception interceptor **swallows the exception**. A blanket
interceptor that returns `null` on every failure will hide real bugs. Handle the exception
types you actually know about and rethrow the rest.
{% /aside %}

## Fallbacks

Supplying a degraded result is legitimate when the caller can use one:

```csharp
public sealed class FallbackToCache : IQueryExceptionInterceptor<GetRates, Rates>
{
    private readonly IMemoryCache _cache;

    public FallbackToCache(IMemoryCache cache) => _cache = cache;

    public ValueTask<Rates?> HandleAsync(
        GetRates query, Rates? result, Exception exception, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        if (exception is HttpRequestException && _cache.TryGetValue<Rates>("rates", out var stale))
            return ValueTask.FromResult<Rates?>(stale);

        throw exception;
    }
}
```

## Ordering

Direct registrations first, then covariant ones, each by `[Weight]` descending — the same
rule as every other stage. The first interceptor that returns a value ends the stage;
interceptors after it do not run.

Put specific translations at a high weight and the blanket logger at a low one, so the logger
sees failures that the specific handlers declined.

## Aborts are not failures

`context.Abort(...)` throws `ExecutionAbortedException`, but the exception stage does **not**
see it. An abort is a decision, not a failure, and exception interceptors exist to handle
failures — so the signal passes through every stage untouched, with its stack intact, and
reaches the caller.

That is deliberate: an exception interceptor that caught aborts would be able to swallow a
deliberate refusal and hand the caller a fabricated result. Catch
`ExecutionAbortedException` at the **call site**, where the decision is yours to act on.

## Coverage

| Interface | `HandleAsync` |
|---|---|
| `ICommandExceptionInterceptor` | `ValueTask<object?>(ICommand, object?, Exception, ErgosfareContext)` |
| `ICommandExceptionInterceptor<TCommand>` | `ValueTask<object?>(TCommand, object?, Exception, ErgosfareContext)` |
| `ICommandExceptionInterceptor<TCommand, TResult>` | `ValueTask<TResult?>(TCommand, TResult?, Exception, ErgosfareContext)` |
| `ICommandExceptionInterceptorFor<TException>` and its `<TCommand, …>` arities | as above, with `TException` in place of `Exception` |
| `IQueryExceptionInterceptor` / `<TQuery, TResult>` / `…For<TException>` | as above |
| `IEventExceptionInterceptor` / `<TEvent>` / `…For<TException>` | `ValueTask<object?>(TEvent, ValueTask, Exception, ErgosfareContext)` |

Next: [Final interceptors](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/final-interceptors).

guides.title: Final interceptors
guides.description: The stage that runs whether the pipeline succeeded or threw — for cleanup, metrics and audit trails.
guides.body:
Final interceptors are new in v2. They run at the very end of a dispatch that ran to its
end — whether the handler succeeded or something threw. That makes them the stage to reach
for when cleanup has to survive a failure.

{% aside type="caution" %}
**An abort is the exception.** `context.Abort(...)` cuts the pipeline where it stands, and
the final stage is downstream of that point, so it does not run. Before v2.3 it did. Cleanup
that must survive an abort belongs in the caller's own `try`/`finally` — see
[Migrating from v2.2 to v2.3](/ergosfare.docs/migration/v2.2-to-v2.3).
{% /aside %}

```csharp
public sealed class RecordDuration : ICommandFinalInterceptor
{
    private readonly IMetrics _metrics;

    public RecordDuration(IMetrics metrics) => _metrics = metrics;

    public ValueTask HandleAsync(
        ICommand command, object? result, Exception? exception, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        if (context.TryGet<long>("started", out var started))
            _metrics.Record(
                command.GetType().Name,
                Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(started),
                failed: exception is not null);

        return ValueTask.CompletedTask;
    }
}
```

## The signature

```csharp
ValueTask HandleAsync(TMessage message, TResult? result, Exception? exception, ErgosfareContext context);
```

Both `result` and `exception` are nullable because **exactly one of them is meaningful** on
any given run:

| Outcome | `result` | `exception` |
|---|---|---|
| Handler succeeded | the result | `null` |
| Handler or interceptor threw | `null` | the exception |
| Exception interceptor supplied a fallback | that fallback | `null` |

An abort has no row: the stage does not run.

{% aside type="tip" %}
**A resultless pipeline still fills the slot.** A command with no result — and every event —
hands the stage `Unit.Value`, the single shared instance of `Stella.Ergosfare.Core.Abstractions.Unit`.
So `result is null` means "no result was produced", and it stays distinct from "this pipeline
has no result type". You can compare against `Unit.Value` by reference; a resultless pipeline
never hands out anything else.
{% /aside %}

Note the return type: plain `ValueTask`, not `ValueTask<T>`. A final interceptor **cannot
change anything**. By the time it runs, the caller's result is decided.

## Where it sits

```
pre*  →  main handler  →  post*        →  final*
                       ↘  exception*  ↗
```

Compare with the other stages:

| Stage | Runs on success | Runs on failure | Runs on abort | Can change the result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pre | before the handler | — | — | rewrites the message |
| Post | yes | no | no | yes |
| Exception | no | yes | no | yes |
| **Final** | **yes** | **yes** | **no** | **no** |

Nothing runs after an abort. That is one rule, not four: the signal cuts the pipeline and
travels to the caller untouched.

## The pairing pattern

A final interceptor is usually the other half of a pre-interceptor. The pre one opens
something, the final one closes it — and the final one closes it even when the pipeline
blew up in between:

```csharp
[Weight(1000)]
public sealed class StartTimer : ICommandPreInterceptor
{
    public ValueTask<object> HandleAsync(ICommand command, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        context.Set("started", Stopwatch.GetTimestamp());
        return ValueTask.FromResult<object>(command);
    }
}
```

Use the context bag rather than a field on the interceptor. Interceptors resolve from the
calling DI scope, so a scoped or singleton instance may be shared across concurrent
dispatches; the context is the only per-dispatch storage.

{% aside type="danger" %}
Do not capture the context past the end of the dispatch. It is pooled and will be handed to
an unrelated dispatch — see
[Execution context](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/execution-context#pooling-and-the-lifetime-rule).
Copy out what you need before returning.
{% /aside %}

## Audit trails

Because a final interceptor sees both outcomes, one registration covers the whole audit:

```csharp
public sealed class AuditEverything : ICommandFinalInterceptor
{
    public async ValueTask HandleAsync(
        ICommand command, object? result, Exception? exception, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        await _audit.WriteAsync(new AuditEntry(
            Operation: command.GetType().Name,
            Succeeded: exception is null,
            Error:     exception?.Message,
            Tenant:    context.TryGet<string>("tenant", out var t) ? t : null));
    }
}
```

## Ordering

Direct registrations first, then covariant ones, each by `[Weight]` descending — the same rule
as every stage. Unlike the exception stage, **every** final interceptor runs; none of them can
end the stage early.

An exception thrown from a final interceptor propagates to the caller and will mask the
original failure. Keep them defensive.

## Coverage

| Interface | `HandleAsync` |
|---|---|
| `ICommandFinalInterceptor` | `ValueTask(ICommand, object?, Exception?, ErgosfareContext)` |
| `ICommandFinalInterceptor<TCommand>` | `ValueTask(TCommand, object?, Exception?, ErgosfareContext)` |
| `ICommandFinalInterceptor<TCommand, TResult>` | `ValueTask(TCommand, TResult?, Exception?, ErgosfareContext)` |
| `IQueryFinalInterceptor` / `<TQuery, TResult>` | as above |
| `IEventFinalInterceptor` / `<TEvent>` | `ValueTask(TEvent, object?, Exception?, ErgosfareContext)` |

Next: [Groups and weights](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/groups-and-weights).

guides.title: Groups and weights
guides.description: Ordering pipeline members with [Weight], scoping them with [Group], and excluding messages with [ExcludeFromPipeline].
guides.body:
Three attributes decide which pipeline members run for a dispatch and in what order. All
three are evaluated when the **pipeline plan** is built — once per `(message type, group
set)` — so none of them costs anything per dispatch.

## `[Weight]` — ordering within a stage

```csharp
[Weight(200)] public sealed class Authorize : ICommandPreInterceptor<DeleteProduct> { … }
[Weight(100)] public sealed class Validate  : ICommandPreInterceptor<DeleteProduct> { … }
[Weight(10)]  public sealed class Log       : ICommandPreInterceptor<DeleteProduct> { … }
```

Higher weight runs **earlier**. The weight is a `uint`, so it cannot be negative; the default
for an unmarked type is 0, which puts it last.

Weight only orders *within a group of equal directness*. The full rule for every stage is:

1. **Direct** entries — registered against the message's own type — ordered by weight descending.
2. **Indirect** entries — matched covariantly through a base type or interface — ordered by weight descending.

A `[Weight(999)]` interceptor registered against `ICommand` still runs after an unweighted one
registered against `DeleteProduct`. Directness wins over weight; see
[Polymorphism](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/polymorphism#direct-before-indirect).

## `[Group]` — scoping to a subset of dispatches

A group tags a handler or interceptor so that a dispatch can ask for it by name:

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Core.Abstractions.Attributes;

[Group("audit")]
public sealed class AuditTrail : ICommandPreInterceptor
{
    public ValueTask<object> HandleAsync(ICommand command, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        _audit.Log(command);
        return ValueTask.FromResult<object>(command);
    }
}
```

The dispatch selects groups through the mediation settings:

```csharp
var settings = new CommandMediationSettings();
settings.Filters.Groups = ["audit"];

await commands.SendAsync(new DeleteProduct(id), settings);
```

With a non-empty filter, **only** pipeline members carrying a matching group participate. An
empty filter — the default — means every registered member participates.

### `GroupSet` — the reusable filter

A settings object per dispatch is an allocation per dispatch, and a fresh string array makes
the grouped executor cache compare group names element-wise every time. `GroupSet` is the
canonical form: `GroupSet.Of(...)` interns equal sequences — same names, same order, ordinal —
so a reused filter matches on a single reference check.

```csharp
static readonly GroupSet Audit = GroupSet.Of("audit");

await commands.SendAsync(new DeleteProduct(id), Audit);
```

Define it once as a static and pass it directly; every mediator facade takes a `GroupSet`
overload. It is also an `IReadOnlyList<string>`, so it drops into the settings form —
`settings.Filters.Groups = Audit;` — and the caches recognise it there too. `GroupSet.Empty`
is the no-filtering default.

A type can belong to several groups:

```csharp
[Group("audit", "compliance")]
public sealed class AuditTrail : ICommandPreInterceptor { … }
```

The default group name for an unmarked type is `"default"`
(`GroupAttribute.DefaultGroupName`).

{% aside type="caution" %}
Group filters apply to **handlers as well as interceptors**. A filter that matches no handler
for the message means nothing handles it. Use groups to select cross-cutting behaviour, not
to route between handlers.
{% /aside %}

Because the group set is part of the plan cache key, the filtering is resolved once per
`(message type, group set)` and never re-walked per dispatch.

{% aside type="note" %}
**Filtering does cost the generated plan, though.** Every generated plan — staged or
single-handler — is consulted only when the dispatch carries no groups at all, so a filtered
dispatch always runs through the general executor. This holds whether the group names are
constants at the call site or computed at runtime; the compiled plans have no group dimension.
Keep group filters off your hottest messages, and use `[ExcludeFromPipeline]` instead when what
you want is "this message skips the blanket interceptors".
{% /aside %}

## `[ExcludeFromPipeline]` — opting a message out

The previous two attributes go on pipeline members. This one goes on a **message**, and
removes it from *covariantly matched* interceptors:

```csharp
[ExcludeFromPipeline]
public sealed record Heartbeat : ICommand;
```

`Heartbeat` no longer picks up the blanket `ICommandPreInterceptor` or anything else matched
through a base type. This is the escape hatch for a high-volume message that should not pay
for the pipeline everything else wants.

Scoped to particular groups:

```csharp
[ExcludeFromPipeline("logging", "metrics")]
public sealed record Tick : ICommand;
```

`Tick` skips covariantly matched members in those two groups and keeps the rest.

Two things are never affected:

- **Interceptors registered for the message type itself.** Someone wrote
  `ICommandPreInterceptor<Heartbeat>` deliberately; it runs.
- **Main handlers.** Excluding a message from the pipeline does not stop it being handled.

## Choosing between them

| You want to… | Use |
|---|---|
| Run authorization before validation | `[Weight]` |
| Run audit interceptors only on the endpoints that need auditing | `[Group]` + a dispatch-time filter |
| Keep one noisy message out of the blanket logger | `[ExcludeFromPipeline]` |
| Decide at startup which handlers exist at all | [discovery keys](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/discovery-keys) |

The last row is the one worth reading twice. Discovery keys are a **registration-time**
decision — the container either selected the handler from the composition table or it did not.
Groups are a **dispatch-time** decision — the handler is selected, and each call chooses
whether it participates.

Next: [Modules and extensions](/ergosfare.docs/core-components/modules-extensions).
